📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after rapidly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked.
  • Sources indicate that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player.
  • Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty promptly again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after rapidly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

Sources indicate that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty promptly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

Industry observers note that while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

In a recent development, for $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

It has been revealed that sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you love old television.

It has been revealed that strands, the Fresh York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

If you're feeling stuck or just don't have 10 or more minutes to figure out today's puzzle, we've got all the NYT Strands hints for today's puzzle you need to progress at your preferred pace.

Some, like The Game Business editor-in-chief Christopher Dring, have speculated that Xbox’s smaller install base has made it harder for some indie devs to “financially justify” launching on Xbox. Others, like John Linneman of Digital Foundry, have countered that Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition is ultimately a minor revision and pointed out that the Xbox Series X version was already available in native 4K, unlike the PS4 and Switch versions.

Google can’t move or manage any money, but it can give you tailored, personalized search results about your finances, like showing where you spend the most, identifying recurring subscriptions you might not be aware of, and suggesting which credit card might be best to use for travel. All you have to do is ask in a search.

Also: I tried Personal Intelligence in Android Auto – and it knew exactly where I wanted to go.

This feature comes just over a week after Google introduced Personal Intelligence to Wallet.

Once your Wallet is connected, it takes a few minutes to fully sync. Once it’s finished, you can ask questions through AI mode in Search.

I decided to give it a try for myself, starting off with a simple query: “Based on my spending, what’s a quick way I can save money?” I could have told you one of the primary culprits, but Google happily responded with what I already knew: far too much of my money goes to fast food and coffee.

“You frequently grab quick-service meals,” the response remarked, pointing out several fast food places that I do indeed frequent, “and specialty coffees throughout the week.” If I just cut that down to two meals and two coffees a week, Gemini explained, I’d save about $30 a week, or $1,500 a year.

Also: This powerful Gemini setting made my AI results way more personal and accurate.

When I asked it to find recurring subscriptions, Gemini noted that I had several monthly charges. What I didn’t ask for, but it did, was to break down those subscriptions into an easy-to-see chart, complete with the name, price, category, the card it’s being charged to, and the timeframe it usually comes out. Gemini even offered a few free alternatives to services I was paying for.

Recent findings suggest that since Gemini also knows what cards are linked to your Wallet, it’s able to offer advice there, too. I’m planning a trip to Fresh York City, so I asked which cards might be best to use for the hotels and airfare. Gemini was able to analyze my card benefits, considering things like rewards and built-in travel insurance, and make a recommendation.

In a recent development, also: Slow Android phone? How to speed it back up in 4 easy steps.

While Gemini Personal Intelligence can access your Gmail to learn more about your spending, it can’t access your bank account. The only information it knows about your finances and spending comes from receipts in your inbox or from your Wallet transaction history. I do use Wallet often (mostly when ordering through online apps), but it’s not quite my go-to option when I’m in a store. Given how useful this feature can be, though, I might just start using Wallet more to give it more information to work with.

Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Sources indicate that players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out latest privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Industry observers note that patch 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Sources indicate that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two fresh options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is right now 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, customers, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is at the moment off, the two “fresh settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

In a recent development, the Motley Fool is the O.G. stock and investment advice website, dating back to the early days of the Internet, when WIRED’s website was still called hotwired.com. It started as a tip sheet in the early ‘90s by brothers Tom and David Gardner, and it rode a wave of hype to become a cult phenomenon, viewed with equal interest and skepticism by the established investment class. Thirty years and a whole bunch of books later, The Motley Fool now feels like the established investment class, with a Stock Advisor subscription service offering stock tips that were shown in a 2017 study led by Penn State to consistently beat the S&P 500.

The Motley Fool is not a single service. Rather, it’s a suite of stock-tips and analysis services, packaged in different bundles. The three main tiers are Stock Advisor ($199), Epic ($499), and Epic Plus ($1,999). Each higher tier offers more stock tips per month, more comprehensive data and research on potential investments, and more sophisticated analysis tools. The Epic Plus tier also offers access to “moneymaker” investment portfolios that are touted to follow Warren Buffett’s investment strategy. Generally, the site advises beginning investors with smaller portfolios to stick to the basic Stock Advisor tips to start out. The Fool also tends to recommend buying at least 50 stocks and holding them for at least 5 years, so it’s not a day-trading tool. Anyway, it’s often hard to find the right links to receive Motley Fool membership discounts. Go to this Motley Fool subscription discount page here for as much as half off the Stock Advisor, Epic, and Epic Plus Bundles for the first year only.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
  • Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you.
  • And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar.".

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

How well Muse works really matters to Meta.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (Â£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse introduced in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that customers and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," remarked David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action prepares.".

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

According to recent reports, and the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.

It has been revealed that I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of massive UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it stated in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch., external.

It has been revealed that "Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike,", external it claims in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.

It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

According to recent reports, I asked Linda - my fresh dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it.".

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control, external once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Moon is looking noticeably less full now, although most of its surface is still illuminated. We're still in the Waning Gibbous phase, with the Moon getting a little smaller each night as we head towards the Third Quarter.

According to recent reports, as of Saturday, Nov. 28, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Gibbous phase, with 81% of its surface visible.

According to recent reports, if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis, Oceanus Procellarum, as well as the Tycho Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Gassendi Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Archimedes Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11 and 15 landing spots, plus the Fra Mauro Highlands.

Recent findings suggest that in North America, the next Full Moon will take place on December 23. In other time zones it will fall on December 24.

Recent findings suggest that it takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a New Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

Upcoming Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

In a recent development, first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

According to recent reports, waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang highlighted the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

It has been revealed that the President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump indicates this is why he needed to act.

Industry observers note that in markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (Â£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

It has been revealed that the brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I’ve written multiple times in the past couple of years about how MacWhisper has become an integral part of my podcast post-production workflow for show notes, episode descriptions, and more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dutch developer Jordi Bruin rolled out an update to his excellent transcription app MacWhisper this week with a much-requested feature: the ability to automatically identify previously named speakers in new recordings. Here are the details.

I’ve written multiple times in the past couple of years about how MacWhisper has become an integral part of my podcast post-production workflow for show notes, episode descriptions, and more.

Which is why I’ve followed the app’s development very closely, and Jordi’s efforts to make it an increasingly powerful tool for casual and power users alike.

In the last few months alone, MacWhisper got a completely redesigned transcript editor, real-time meeting transcription, significantly improved speaker detection, deeper integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Spotlight, and support for multiple new transcription models.

This week, MacWhisper got updated to version 16, packing several improvements, chief among them the ability to recognize speakers based on their voices in previous transcripts.

Recent findings suggest that until now, while MacWhisper could distinguish between different speakers in a recording (a process known as speaker diarization), consumers still had to assign names to each new transcription manually. With MacWhisper 16, that is no longer necessarily the case.

Now, MacWhisper creates a set of voiceprints for the speakers consumers have previously identified, and uses them as a reference when processing upcoming recordings. Depending on the confidence level of a match, MacWhisper will either automatically assign the speaker’s name or ask the user to confirm their identity.

According to Bruin, as people transcribe more recordings featuring the same people, MacWhisper gets better at recognizing their voices. All voiceprint processing and storage happen on-device, which is a great touch.

The feature also works with existing transcripts, which is fantastic for longtime MacWhisper users such as myself. A new Voice Recognition section in the app’s settings lets users generate voiceprints from existing transcripts, clear a speaker’s stored voice data, or turn the feature off altogether.

Importantly, voice recognition also works with live meeting transcriptions, although automatic name assignments happen once the meeting ends.

The upcoming feature requires a MacWhisper Pro license, an Apple silicon Mac, and on-device transcription with speaker detection enabled.

#4635. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
  • Recent findings suggest that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024.
  • It has been revealed that as of October 2026, data center developers have declared plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

Recent findings suggest that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

It has been revealed that as of October 2026, data center developers have declared plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” notes Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a fresh industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

It has been revealed that rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” states Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Sources indicate that behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont claims.

Industry observers note that even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building fresh fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi claims.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.).

In a recent development, utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

In a recent development, today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

Industry observers note that bloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

According to recent reports, and while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

In a recent development, there’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

According to recent reports, creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

In a recent development, while the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

In a recent development, “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp indicates. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022.
  • The timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out.
  • According to recent reports, utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

The timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner stated access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint states.

According to recent reports, utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

Sources indicate that the complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the organization to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Industry observers note that utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

The Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the firm did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.
  • US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
  • Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about.".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

Trump has noted he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.

With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also revealed it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either.".

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the firm as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

In a recent development, the company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, its chairman, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board mentioned it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

On Monday, Trump remarked he had spoken to the tech giant's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.

Republican Congressman Don Bacon mentioned Nvidia should have "ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts stated Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Last year, Counterpoint Research found that during China’s Double 11 shopping period, strong demand for the iPhone 17 lineup helped drive a 3% year-over-year increase in smartphone sales in the country.

This year, Apple once again came out on top, though rising smartphone prices and limited promotional discounts weighed on overall consumer demand.

According to the report, Apple saw an 8% year-over-year decline in iPhone sales during the promotional period. Still, compared with the market-wide 17% drop, Apple fared considerably better than most of its competitors.

Furthermore, Apple accounted for six of the 10 bestselling smartphone models during the promotional period, including all five of the top spots.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max topped the ranking, while the newly launched iPhone Duo came in ninth despite going on sale only on October 23, nearly two weeks after the shopping festival kicked off on October 12.

Counterpoint also noted that Huawei “was the only major OEM to record growth, up 29% YoY, driven mainly by the Enjoy 90 Pro Max and Pura X View, with the new Enjoy 100 series providing an additional boost.” The Enjoy 90 Pro Max was the only Huawei model to make the top 10, coming in sixth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
  • Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
  • In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei mentioned, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first declared the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche remarked in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.".

The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.

Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

Industry observers note that "Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board.".

Sources indicate that sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig mentioned there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the manufacturer's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he noted.

WABetaInfo noted that after long-pressing the send button, consumers who have access to the new feature can select between scheduling the message and sending it as a view-once message.

Recipients can then tap the message to read it in a separate interface, with WhatsApp blocking screenshots, screen recordings, copying, and forwarding. Once the recipient closes the message, neither party can access its contents again.

In another test rolling out to iPhone beta users, WhatsApp is making a slight change to the app’s tab bar, removing the text labels that appear below each icon while preserving its existing Liquid Glass design.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, MGM Resorts and BetMGM have canceled their memberships in the National Council on Problem Gambling because the group accepted Kalshi.
  • The companies’ letter to the council is dated Nov.
  • It has been revealed that the companies wrote that they no longer hold the principles the group once stood for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, MGM Resorts and BetMGM have canceled their memberships in the National Council on Problem Gambling because the group accepted Kalshi. Their exit brings licensed operators into a split over prediction markets that had so far involved regulators and state problem-gambling councils.

The companies’ letter to the council is dated Nov. 18. Stephen Martino, MGM Resorts’ senior vice president and chief compliance officer, signed it alongside Rhea Loney, BetMGM’s chief compliance officer. It went to interim executive director Charles Jeffers and board president Derek Longmeier.

It has been revealed that the companies wrote that they no longer hold the principles the group once stood for. They argued that promoting gambling as a way out of financial trouble runs against responsible gaming principles. The letter also charged that Kalshi disregards state gambling laws when it sells sports event contracts in states whose regulators consider them unlicensed gambling.

Sources indicate that MGM and BetMGM are the first gambling operators to confirm they left specifically over the council’s work with Kalshi, SBC Americas reported. The Ohio Casino Control Commission had already ended its membership. The Michigan Gaming Control Board withdrew its membership in a July 1, 2026 letter. The Nevada Council on Problem Gambling and Washington’s Evergreen Council on Problem Gambling also left.

The council unveiled the deal at the center of the dispute on May 18, 2026. Besides its funding commitment, Kalshi received a seat in the NCPG’s Leadership Circle. That group is made up of top partners that help fund the organization.

Sources indicate that the Nov. 18 letter sets out the main grievances licensed operators hold against prediction markets. Kalshi lets 18-year-olds trade. Most licensed sportsbooks require bettors to be 21. Prediction markets pay little in state taxes, which leaves less money for problem-gambling programs. They also sit outside state self-exclusion programs.

According to recent reports, each of those points touches the core work of a harm-reduction body. The fight over whether prediction markets count as gambling has now reached the main US problem-gambling group.

“No organization should understand the risks Kalshi and other prediction markets pose to responsible gaming more clearly and urgently than NCPG,”– MGM/BetMGM while ending membership in the National Council on Problem Gambling.https://t.co/7A0Wi2AIFo via @reviewjournal.

— David Danzis (@AC2Vegas_Danzis) November 22, 2026.

The NCPG has not backed down. The group describes its prediction-market work as a way to tackle newly introduced sources of gambling harm. It says that work does not endorse particular companies or how they do business. In a Friday statement, the NCPG noted the risks of prediction markets will not go away when organizations refuse to engage. It added that leaving over this work may send a political message but does nothing to prevent gambling-related harm.

It’s infuriating that Google still hasn’t released a upcoming Nest Hub, and it makes Amazon’s Black Friday discounts for Echo Show smart displays pretty darn tempting.

Google has always taken a pretty conservative approach to smart home hardware, but the gap in Nest Hub releases is getting more than a bit frustrating at this point. Nest Hub’s last hardware enhancement was in 2021, and the Nest Hub Max even further back in 2019. There’s some hope on the horizon, but the competition hasn’t slowed down. That context in mind, Amazon’s Echo Show series sure is tempting right now.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t just a Black Friday deal post. It’s also me as someone who’s deeply invested in the Google Home ecosystem being annoyed there’s no Nest Hub sequel, nothing to replace the aging hardware in my home, and genuinely being tempted by the alternatives.

How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 saw record retail sales in its first full day of release, hitting $3.8bn (Â£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.
  • Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem â and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.
  • Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 saw record retail sales in its first full day of release, hitting $3.8bn (Â£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.

Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem â and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.

The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch â 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

This time it may not have that luxury â in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.

These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6.

Barely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.

For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.

For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?

The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.

Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit and whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a upcoming game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.

This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" â something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a latest painting".

It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.

When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled".

"The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC.

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a fresh game based on an existing one.

The second approach â reverse engineering â involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.

One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code.

Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".

Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.

A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.

Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.

In a recent development, earlier in November, Cyberleek â a hacker or group of hackers â released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.

It gave those working on an unofficial PC version a crucial new starting point.

"Now people are using AI to try and decompile it, make a modified version that could run on PC, and compile a fresh version," stated Brown.

Reverse-engineering projects have made it possible to bring full games such as Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.

Since the leak, several groups have posted claims of their progress on platforms such as X, ranging from getting the game to boot up to making it run at a stable rate.

One attempt seen by the BBC on X purported to have some of the game running nearly as smoothly as it does on console, albeit on a high-end PC.

Accounts and sites have even sprung up to track the various attempts, excitedly sharing clips of the latest milestone passed and scoring their efforts.

Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build, and neither has responded to the BBC's request for a statement.

However, Take-Two has issued take, externaldown notices, external of public projects aiming to port the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub.

Tech Life: One hundred years of AI.

Sources indicate that laura Cress talks to game designers who say their unreleased new game was copied using AI. And Shiona McCallum reports on a new AI police chatbot.

News of the leak has been celebrated by some gamers on Reddit, who resent having to wait for the PC release.

"Why should the PC players have to wait half a year if you can develop the game in weeks as shown so far!" wrote one gamer, external.

"Will be funny when the decomp runs way better than whatever Rockstar can make," stated another.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, stated part of the reason why the games are often released on PCs months after consoles is that PC versions are "complex" with "different hardware configurations", as opposed to the more standardised set-up of consoles.

He added there could also be a more commercial reason, as Rockstar can "have a second moment when the PC version is ready".

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, external, the chief executive of Take-Two Interactive, Strauss Zelnick, said while piracy was a "fact of life" in the entertainment business, it had until now been "less of an problem" for video games due to their "file sizes and complexity".

In a recent development, however, Zelnick also reportedly told an investor Q&A that the organization was "utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and... legal activities appropriately".

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics.

He added that decompiling code could be legal within limits, such as for educational purposes, but "as soon as you attempt to use it to redistribute or repackage existing software", then this is "largely illegal".

"In most cases, decompiling or recompiling code is likely to involve unauthorised use of the game IP," said Aaron Treble, a UK intellectual property lawyer for Lewis Silkin.

Anthropic has reportedly since told Claude Code to steer away from recreating specific existing games, external, saying this would breach its usage policy.

Despite this, people are continuing to work on an unofficial PC game, hoping to make it playable before Rockstar releases the official version.

"Seeing as this has already affected industry giants with very deep pockets, the proverbial bear has been poked," stated Brown.

"We'll have to see how it reacts.".

Tech Report: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical problems in recent weeks.
  • The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter.
  • The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical problems in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

In a recent development, one of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA remarked in a statement last week.

“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the challenges and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA stated.

It has been revealed that perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention to recovering the primary radio, NASA mentioned.

“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”.

The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.

It has been revealed that the situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.

Sources indicate that “Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA stated. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.

Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, noted Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.

That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is that ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.

According to recent reports, odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.

Industry observers note that NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software problem caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.

MAVEN’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on the spacecraft’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.

NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.

NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office. The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.

It has been revealed that another Mars mission, SkyFall, could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.

A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.

Sources indicate that NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The firm has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.

In a recent development, after Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless. The AP reports that Los Angeles Unified School Distict (LAUSD), which enrolls about half a million students, quietly disabled Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices.

In a recent development, although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results. That prompted a local advocacy group, Schools Beyond Screens LA, to ask parents to send video evidence. The group then received confirmation from the school district that AI Overviews were indeed disabled, albeit without details on the exact method used. (Third-party tools seem a likely candidate.).

According to recent reports, the move came after a Nov. 13 meeting of LAUSD's AI committee, where several Schools Beyond Screens members spoke. A few days later, the AI summaries had vanished from school devices. The district describes the change as temporary and about keeping students' experience "age-appropriate and safe.".

Earlier this month, Google walked back one policy on AI in schools that had sparked a backlash: switching on its Gemini chatbot by default for many K-12 students. (Google's AI tools will now be opt-in for students.) But at the same time, the company insisted that the connection between search and AI was a different story. Google VP & General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, told The Latest York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that if a district blocked AI, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available.".

If that sounds like Google throwing its weight around to justify its massive AI spending, well, some of the manufacturer's own workers might agree. Over 500 of them signed a petition earlier this month, asking their employer to reconsider the strict requirements.

If Google doesn't back down, it could be risking a significant loss of business. Upcoming York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering switching search engines if it comes to that.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI has filed counterclaims against Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers not to work on OpenAI’s devices and using broad employment agreements to stop engineers joining OpenAI, Bloomberg reported. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging theft of hardware trade secrets.

In a recent development, openAI states Apple has pushed suppliers not to work on its devices, Bloomberg reported. It made the claims in a court filing in San Jose on Friday, hitting back at Apple’s trade-secrets lawsuit.

“Apple has responded to OpenAI’s anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI,” the manufacturer said in the filing.

Sources indicate that according to OpenAI, Apple asks suppliers to name their OpenAI projects and the staff on them who once worked for Apple. It then tries to keep anyone who has worked on OpenAI products off Apple jobs. That makes suppliers wary of putting staff on OpenAI work.

One supplier moved its OpenAI work to the night shift so it would not overlap with Apple work, which raised OpenAI’s costs, the filing states. Others have moved meetings with OpenAI so Apple would not see them.

OpenAI also takes aim at the contracts Apple staff sign. It indicates they treat almost everything workers learn as secret and stop them hiring away Apple staff for a year. It repeats its claim that a former worker who returned to Apple took more than 100 files about an unreleased OpenAI device.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg. It has stated before that it found no evidence for OpenAI’s claims.

Apple sued in July. It notes OpenAI and its hardware chief Tang Tan used former Apple staff to get its secrets, and that OpenAI had a shared supplier copy an Apple metal-finishing method. In October, OpenAI agreed not to use the files Apple says were taken while the case goes on.

The fight hangs over OpenAI’s aims to sell devices designed with Jony Ive, starting with a doughnut-shaped speaker. The two once worked together to bring ChatGPT to Siri, a partnership that has since turned sour.
